mcqs.question: A 10-minute analytics report runs under MVCC while thousands of writes commit to the same table. Why does the report never block, and never get blocked by, those writes?
options: The report takes a shared lock on the whole table for its full 10 minutes
The writes are queued and only applied after the report finishes
The report reads a fixed snapshot — the newest row versions committed before it started — while writers keep creating new versions independently
MVCC disables all writes to any table currently being read
mcqs.explanation: MVCC gives the report a consistent snapshot of committed versions as of when it started; writers keep creating newer versions the report simply never looks at, so neither side blocks the other. There's no table-wide lock, no queuing of writes, and writes aren't disabled during reads.

mcqs.question: An engine's wait-for graph shows transaction A waiting on a lock held by B, and B waiting on a lock held by C, with no edge back to A. What does this tell you?
options: This is a deadlock and one of the three transactions must be killed
The wait-for graph is meaningless without also checking CPU usage
This is only a deadlock if all three transactions are on different rows
There is no cycle, so every transaction will eventually be able to proceed once the ones ahead of it finish
mcqs.explanation: A deadlock requires a cycle in the wait-for graph; a chain with no edge back to the start (A to B to C) just means A and B are waiting their turn, not stuck forever. Row identity and CPU usage aren't what the wait-for graph is checking — it's purely about cycles.

mcqs.question: Why do most mainstream relational databases use deadlock detection rather than a fixed lock-wait timeout?
options: Detection only aborts a transaction when a real wait-for cycle actually exists, whereas a timeout also kills transactions that were merely slow, not deadlocked
Timeouts are impossible to implement correctly in a multi-threaded database
Detection uses less CPU than checking a timer
Timeouts can only be used with table-level locks, not row-level locks
mcqs.explanation: Detection precisely identifies a cycle before acting, avoiding false positives on transactions that are simply waiting behind legitimate, resolvable contention. A timer check is actually cheap, timeouts aren't restricted to table-level locks, and timeouts are perfectly implementable — they're just blunter.

mcqs.question: A batch job processes pairs of rows in whatever order they arrive from an upstream queue, locking both rows per pair. Under concurrent load, transactions deadlock several times a day. What is the most direct, permanent fix?
options: Increase the deadlock_timeout so the engine waits longer before detecting a cycle
Disable locking for this job entirely by using Read Uncommitted
Sort each pair's row IDs into a canonical order before locking, regardless of the order they arrived in
Add more application servers to process the queue in parallel
mcqs.explanation: The root cause is inconsistent lock ordering; enforcing a canonical order removes the specific cross-wait cycle structurally. A longer detection timeout just delays discovery, disabling locking removes correctness guarantees rather than fixing ordering, and more app servers would increase concurrent load and likely worsen the deadlock rate.

mcqs.question: A Postgres database has had autovacuum effectively disabled for months due to misconfiguration, and a long-running transaction has also been open the whole time. What is the most serious risk this combination creates?
options: Slightly higher disk usage, with no other consequences
The database will silently switch to a locking-only mode instead of MVCC
Read queries will start returning dirty, uncommitted data
Severe table bloat from unreclaimed dead row versions, compounding toward transaction ID wraparound risk that can force the database to refuse new writes
mcqs.explanation: Disabled autovacuum plus a long-open transaction pinning the cleanup horizon is exactly the combination that produces severe bloat and, left long enough, pushes toward transaction ID wraparound — a real outage risk. Postgres doesn't switch off MVCC, and this scenario doesn't cause dirty reads; the effect is far worse than 'slightly higher disk usage.'

mcqs.question: You see several queries stuck for over a minute in production, but no deadlock error appears in the database logs. What does the absence of a deadlock error tell you?
options: This is lock contention, not a deadlock — there's no wait-for cycle, so the engine has nothing to detect and resolve automatically
The engine's deadlock detector must be broken, since any stuck query is a deadlock
It means the queries are using MVCC and therefore cannot deadlock by definition
The deadlock will still be logged, just after a longer delay than usual
mcqs.explanation: A genuine deadlock is a cycle, and engines detect and resolve cycles automatically within their detection interval, logging an explicit error. Stuck queries with no such error are waiting on contention with no cycle, not an undetected deadlock. MVCC governs reads, not whether write-lock deadlocks can occur, and there's no hidden delayed deadlock log here.
